Pied-à-terre tax · Co-op shares

Co-op shares and the pied-à-terre tax

How whole-building city values convert into an apartment figure, with an on-page share calculator.

Cooperative apartments do not get separate tax-lot market values on the Department of Finance assessment roll. Under New York Real Property Tax Law § 581, the city values the entire co-op building as a rental property. Each apartment's figure for the non-primary residence surcharge comes from multiplying that building value by the apartment's fraction of corporate shares.

Estimate an apartment from its shares

Enter the co-op building's FY2027 city market value (find it on our live checker or in the co-op building directory) together with the unit's shares and total building shares (or ownership percentage).

2.500% of $71,230,000 = $1,780,750 ($780,750 above $1M line) · Phase 1 bracket: 4% ($71,230/yr illustrative if non-primary).

Runs strictly in your browser; zero inputs leave this page.

Important details on the co-op roll

  • Commercial income lifts some co-op averages. When a co-op building contains ground-floor retail or offices, that value sits inside the single building BBL on the public roll.
  • No published unit shares on DOF open data. Because public city files record total apartments (coop_apts) without apartment share schedules, our 396 listed co-op pages show the plain average per apartment.
  • Same Phase 1 brackets and exemptions as condos. $1M–$3M (4%), $3M–$5M (5.25%), over $5M (6.5%), on the whole unit share value; primary residences and 1-year tenants are exempt (full exemption rules).
  • Who can file Form TC107. A co-op corporation may file a Form TC107 surcharge appeal for a unit owner by March 1, 2027 (TC107 guide).

Deadline to challenge the value

To contest the market value behind the surcharge, file Tax Commission Form TC107 by March 1, 2027 for condos and co-ops, or March 15, 2027 for houses. The form cannot be used to protest the assessed value. See the TC107 guide or the deadline timeline.
